extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners advising applicants)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating patent claims for obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103, including the Graham factual inquiries, acceptable rationales for rejections, searching/prior-art scope, treatment of level of ordinary skill, applicant rebuttal, and analogous-art/joint-ownership rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory obviousness standard (35 U.S.C. 103)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent may not be obtained though the invention is not identically disclosed under section 102, if the differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious at the time the invention was made to a person having ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentability shall not be negatived by the manner in which the invention was made. Subsections (b)-(c) provide special biotech/process/ownership/joint-research provisions; an obviousness rejection is grounded in the statutory language and appropriate prior art categories (e.g., 102(a),(b),(e)).

rubrics_metrics.name: KSR flexible approach / role of common sense and TSM
rubrics_metrics.description: KSR reaffirmed a flexible approach to obviousness, warning against overly rigid application of the teaching-suggestion-motivation (TSM) test and emphasizing that common sense and ordinary creativity of a person of ordinary skill are relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TSM remains a valid rationale but should not be applied rigidly; examiners may rely on common sense or reasoned explanation that avoids conclusory generalizations. Use TSM where appropriate, but consider other rationales as listed. The analysis should avoid hindsight and be explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factual inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: The three basic factual inquiries from Graham: (A) determining the scope and content of the prior art; (B) ascertaining differences between the claimed invention and the prior art; and (C) resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factors — including any available secondary considerations — 'define the inquiry that controls' and may be reordered case-by-case; all underlying factual findings should be articulated in the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations (objective evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence (secondary considerations) relevant to obviousness may include commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, and unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such evidence may be presented in the specification, accompanying application, or timely during prosecution; its weight is case-by-case and the mere presentation of evidence is not dispositive. Examiners must evaluate and articulate weight given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners as factfinders — requirement to articulate findings and rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel must include findings of fact supporting the state of the art and teachings of applied references and must provide an explanation to support any obviousness rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 35 U.S.C. 132 requires notification of reasons for rejection. Findings of fact and reasoned explanations avoid conclusory statements and prevent appeals; unclear or unarticulated factual bases may be fatal on review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and content of prior art — claim interpretation and broadest reasonable interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the scope and content of the prior art after first understanding the invention disclosed and claimed by reading the specification and claims; claims must be given the 'broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once claim scope is determined, determine what to search for and where. Search should cover claimed subject matter and disclosed features reasonably expected to be claimed (see MPEP §904).

rubrics_metrics.name: What to search for in prior-art searches
rubrics_metrics.description: Search should cover the claimed subject matter and disclosed features which might reasonably be expected to be claimed; preferred searches will seek references that provide teaching or suggestion to combine if they exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although a rejection need not be based on a teaching/suggestion to combine, examiners should look for such references when available. See MPEP §904–§904.03 for search procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where to search — analogous/pertinent fields and cross-field references
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art for 35 U.S.C. 103 can be from the applicant's field of endeavor or from fields reasonably pertinent to the particular problem; works from other fields may be considered where design incentives or market forces make variations predictable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not limit searches only to the problem the patentee was trying to solve; consider reasonable pertinent arts and references from other fields that address similar design incentives or problems (KSR).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascertaining differences between claim and prior art (claim interpretation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ascertaining differences requires interpreting the claim language and considering the invention and prior art as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §2111 for claim interpretation guidance; comparisons should be holistic, identifying which claim limitations remain unshown or how they differ from the prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolving level of ordinary skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: An obviousness rejection should include an indication of the level of ordinary skill, which is a hypothetical person presumed to know the relevant art at the time of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider factors such as (1) types of problems encountered in the art; (2) prior art solutions; (3) rapidity of innovations; (4) sophistication of the technology; and (5) educational level of active workers. Examiners may use their technical expertise; note that a person of ordinary skill is assumed to have ordinary creativity and may fit multiple patents together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding hindsight — content of prior art determined at time invention made
rubrics_metrics.description: Content of the prior art and the obviousness inquiry must be judged as of the time the invention was made to avoid impermissible hindsight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should cast the mind back to the relevant time and not rely on knowledge gained after the invention. See MPEP §2145 for rebuttal arguments alleging hindsight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationales to support an obviousness rejection (exemplary list)
rubrics_metrics.description: A non-exhaustive list of rationales that may support obviousness: (A) combining prior-art elements by known methods to yield predictable results; (B) simple substitution of known elements to obtain predictable results; (C) using a known technique to improve similar devices; (D) applying a known technique to a known device ready for improvement; (E) 'obvious to try' — choosing from a finite set of predictable solutions with a reasonable expectation of success; (F) variations prompted by known work in another field when predictable; (G) some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art to modify or combine references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List is illustrative, not exhaustive. Examiners must articulate why a chosen rationale applies and how it makes the claim obvious; see MPEP §§2143–2144 for examples and additional guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to provide articulated, non-conclusory reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejections on obviousness cannot be sustained by mere conclusory statements; there must be some articulated reasoning with a rational underpinning for the legal conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite and explain why differences would have been obvious to the person of ordinary skill. Reference In re Kahn and KSR's admonition; avoid generic assertions of common knowledge without factual underpinning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant's reply obligations (37 CFR 1.111(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants must distinctly and specifically point out supposed errors in the Office action and reply to every ground of objection and rejection; replies must present arguments pointing out the specific distinctions believed to render the claims patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A traverse disputing factual findings must include a reasoned statement explaining the alleged error; mere statements that a prima facie case is not established or unsupported claims of misuse of common knowledge are substantively inadequate and may lead to final rejection (see MPEP §706.07(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of applicant's rebuttal evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should consider all timely rebuttal evidence submitted by applicants when reevaluating any obviousness determination, including secondary considerations and evidence of unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rebuttal evidence may demonstrate that: (A) one of ordinary skill could not have combined the claimed elements by known methods (e.g., technological difficulties); (B) the elements in combination do not merely perform their separate functions; or (C) the claimed combination produced unexpected results. After rebuttal, reconsider initial determinations and review all rejections and their bases for continued viability.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 103(c) — evidence and burden for common ownership/joint research
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant seeking benefits of 35 U.S.C. 103(c) has the burden of establishing that subject matter which qualifies as prior art only under 102(e),(f),(g) and the claimed invention were, when the invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person (or were within a qualifying joint research agreement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For joint research benefits applicant must show (A) invention made by/on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the invention date; (B) invention resulted from activities within the scope of the agreement; and (C) the application discloses or is amended to disclose the parties' names. See MPEP §706.02(l)(2) for requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous art requirement for applied references
rubrics_metrics.description: To be proper for use in an obviousness rejection, a reference must be analogous prior art: either (1) from the same field of endeavor as the claimed invention (even if addressing a different problem), or (2) reasonably pertinent to the problem faced by the inventor (even if not in the same field).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must determine what constitutes analogous prior art when analyzing obviousness (see In re Bigio). The Supreme Court's KSR decision confirms that cross-field references may be analogous when variations would be predictable to one of ordinary skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admitted prior art and use in obviousness determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Admitted prior art may be relied upon for both anticipation and obviousness determinations, regardless of whether it otherwise qualifies under statutory categories of 35 U.S.C. 102.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admissions in the specification or prosecution history can be treated as prior art; see Riverwood Int’l Corp. v. R.A. Jones and Constant v. AMD for precedent. See MPEP §2129 for admissions as prior art discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art substantive content and enabling disclosure considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantive content of the prior art includes issues such as availability of inoperative devices, the extent to which a prior-art disclosure must be enabling, preferred vs. broad embodiments, and admissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should consult MPEP §2121–§2129 for case law and guidance on substantive content and how much detail from prior art can be relied upon in obviousness/anticipation analyses.
